description:
Start with a real project

Write short lines you would say aloud. Mark unfamiliar pronunciations and break up sentences that are hard to read in one breath.

Review the first version

Compare voices against the same excerpt and listen without background music. Check emphasis and whether the voice fits the audience.

Check the final result

Match the narration to the scene timing. Check the voice and export rights for the project before using the final audio in public.

Frequently asked questions

How should I test a voice?

Render a short sample with the hardest words in the script and compare it against your video timing.

Browse related tools on SEOGBTools.

Test a voice with your actual script

Pick twenty seconds from the most demanding part of your script. Include a product name, a number, and a phrase that requires a pause. For a course introduction, the test might include the name of a software feature and an instruction to open a particular screen. For a product demo, it might include a measurement and the name of a part shown in close-up.

Listen to two or three voices using exactly the same text. Check whether the listener can understand the words on the first pass. A calm voice can work well for instructions if it leaves time for viewers to follow the screen. A faster reading may fit a short introduction if it keeps key details clear. Write down the voice and the version of the script you tested.

Edit pronunciation and pacing

Use plain words where they suit the audience, and keep terms the listener will see in a menu or on a product label. If a name sounds wrong, try writing a short phonetic guide in the working script or use a pronunciation control if your editor offers one. Keep the correct spelling in the captions and in your approved source script.

Put a pause where the viewer needs time to act. A voiceover for changing a setting should give the instruction before the cursor moves to the next menu. Watch the clip with the narration in place. If the instructions get ahead of the screen, shorten the line or give the shot more time. Make changes a scene at a time so the next edit is easy to check.

Prepare the final audio for delivery

Export a short sample before producing the entire project. Open it in the video editor you expect to use and check the audio format and volume. Listen on phone speakers and headphones. If music makes a word hard to hear, lower the music under that line or move the cue.

Confirm the usage rights for the voice and the intended project. A training video, public advertisement, and client deliverable can have different requirements. If you are comparing group buy access, ask SEOGBTools which voices, languages, and export options are included. Keep the approved script and final audio in your project folder.

For related workflows, see ElevenLabs and Murf AI.

Build a voiceover for a real product demo

Imagine you are making a one-minute demo of a desktop microphone. Your opening shot shows the microphone plugged into a laptop, but a first-time viewer still needs to know where to select it. Begin with the step that changes what the viewer sees. Say, “Open your sound settings and select the USB microphone.” Give the viewer enough time to find the setting before you explain how to test it.

Make a simple table in your production notes with a shot name, a line of narration, and a time range. Separate the instruction from the result. The line about choosing the device belongs over the settings screen. The line about hearing a recording belongs over the playback controls. This helps when you need to replace one scene without recording the whole script again.

Use the same test line when comparing voices. A demo needs clear instructions and time for someone to follow the screen. A promotional clip can move faster because the viewer only needs to understand one idea. Compare a neutral read with a warmer read and choose the one that supports the task. Play it without the video once to hear where the wording is confusing.

Prepare separate files for the final edit

Give each export a name that matches its place in the timeline. A series of files called intro, setup, test, and closing will be easier to replace than one long recording. Keep the approved wording next to each file name. If a client asks for a change, you can find the exact line and check whether the new wording still fits the shot.

Listen to the finished video on a phone and on headphones. Check the first word after each music cue and the last word before a cut. If the narration is clear with headphones but hard to hear on a phone, adjust the background music during speech. Check captions against the final audio after making changes to the timing.

Can I use an AI voice in a paid campaign?

Check the license for the specific voice, the intended use, and your access plan. If the campaign uses a voice based on a real person, make sure you have their permission for that use. Save the approval with the project notes.
